question: My mom just turned 65 and is signing up for Medicare. How much will her Part B premium be each month in 2026, and is there anything that could make it higher?
expected_answer: The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90 a month, and most people pay that standard amount. She would pay more only if she owes an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA), which applies when the modified adjusted gross income on the tax return from 2 years ago was above the limit: for 2026, a 2024 income above $109,000 filing individually or $218,000 married filing jointly. The handbook points to Medicare.gov for IRMAA details and to SSA.gov/medicare/lower-irmaa to disagree with the extra charge.

evidence.quote: The standard Part B premium amount in 2026 is $202.90. Most people pay the standard Part B premium amount every month.
For 2026, if your modified adjusted gross income for 2024 was above $109,000 if you file individually or $218,000 if you’re married and file jointly, then you may pay an IRMAA.

question: Dad has Original Medicare and no other insurance. He spent 5 days in the hospital and then went straight into a skilled nursing facility for 30 days. What will he owe for that in 2026?
expected_answer: About $3,906 in Part A charges. He pays the $1,736 Part A deductible once for the benefit period, and hospital days 1–60 cost $0 a day after it, so the 5 hospital days add nothing more. He does not pay the deductible a second time at the skilled nursing facility because he already paid it in the same benefit period; SNF days 1–20 are $0 a day and days 21–100 are $217 a day, so the 10 days over 20 cost 10 × $217 = $2,170. A correct answer must give the $1,736 deductible, the $217 daily SNF rate, and the fact that the deductible is not charged twice in one benefit period.

evidence.quote: Each time you start a new benefit period, you must pay $1,736 (in 2026) before Medicare starts to pay.
Days 1–60: After you pay the $1,736 Part A deductible, you pay $0 each day.
Days 1–20: You pay $0 each day after you pay the $1,736 amount.
Days 21–100: You pay $217 each day.
you don’t have to pay the Part A deductible for skilled nursing facility care if you already paid it for care you got in a hospital during the same benefit period

question: What are the 2026 income and resource limits for qualifying for Extra Help with Medicare drug costs?
expected_answer: The handbook does not give the 2026 limits. The only limits it prints are the 2025 ones (single person: yearly income less than $23,475 and resources less than $17,600; married person living with a spouse and no other dependents: less than $31,725 and less than $35,130), and it says the 2026 income and resource limits can be found on Medicare.gov. A correct answer says the 2026 figures are not in the handbook and points to Medicare.gov, and may add SSA.gov/extrahelp to apply or 1-800-MEDICARE.

question: My mother is having trouble hearing. Does Original Medicare pay for hearing aids, or for the exam to fit them?
expected_answer: No to both. Original Medicare does not cover hearing aids or the exams for fitting them, so she would have to pay for those herself. What it does cover is a diagnostic hearing and balance (fall risk) exam that her doctor or other health care provider orders to see if she needs medical treatment, and one audiologist visit every 12 months without an order for non-acute hearing conditions; for those she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount and the Part B deductible applies.

Medicare covers diagnostic hearing and balance (fall risk) exams if your doctor or health care provider orders them to see if you need medical treatment.

You pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. The Part B deductible applies.
Hearing aids and exams for fitting them.

question: I'm 68 and still working at a company with 12 employees, and I have the company health plan as well as Medicare. Which one pays my medical bills first?
expected_answer: Medicare pays first. The handbook's coordination chart says that if you are 65 or older and have group health plan coverage based on your or your spouse's current employment and the employer has fewer than 20 employees, Medicare pays first. The group health plan would pay first only if the employer had 20 or more employees, or had fewer than 20 but was part of a multi-employer plan that includes other employers with 20 or more employees.

evidence.quote: If you’re 65 or older, have group health plan coverage based on your or your spouse’s current employment, and the employer has fewer than 20 employees... Medicare pays first.
the employer has 20 or more employees OR your employer has fewer than 20 employees but is part of a multi-employer plan

question: My mom turns 65 on March 12. When can she sign up for Medicare without paying a penalty, and when would her coverage start?
expected_answer: Her Initial Enrollment Period for Part A and Part B is the 7-month window that begins 3 months before the month she turns 65 and ends 3 months after it, so December through June. (The shifted window only applies if the birthday falls on the first of the month, and hers does not.) If she signs up during the first 3 months, December through February, coverage generally begins on March 1, the first day of her birthday month. If she signs up in March itself or in April, May or June, coverage starts the first day of the month after she signs up.

evidence.quote: Generally, you can first sign up for Part A and/or Part B during the 7-month period that begins 3 months before the month you turn 65 and ends 3 months after the month you turn 65.
in most cases, your coverage begins the first day of your birthday month
If you sign up the month you turn 65 or during the last 3 months of your Initial Enrollment Period, your coverage starts the first day of the month after you sign up.

question: My husband is retiring in April and I'm 67 and covered by his employer's health plan. How long will I have to sign up for Part B, and does taking COBRA buy me more time?
expected_answer: You can sign up any time you are still covered by the group health plan, and then during the 8-month Special Enrollment Period that begins the month after the employment ends or the coverage ends, whichever happens first. Signing up in that window usually means no late enrollment penalty. COBRA does not extend it: COBRA is not coverage based on current employment, so the 8 months run from the end of the employment-based coverage whether or not you take COBRA, and you generally will not get another Special Enrollment Period when the COBRA ends.

evidence.quote: During the 8-month period that begins the month after the employment ends or the coverage ends, whichever happens first
Usually, you won’t have to pay a late enrollment penalty if you sign up during a Special Enrollment Period.
After coverage based on current employment ends, you have 8 months to sign up for Part B without a penalty, whether or not you choose COBRA.
You generally aren’t eligible for a Special Enrollment Period to sign up for Medicare when that COBRA coverage ends.

question: I turn 65 on August 14, I'm still working, and I put money into a health savings account through my job. If I sign up for Medicare during my Initial Enrollment Period, when does my last HSA contribution have to be?
expected_answer: July, the month before you turn 65. The handbook's chart says that if you sign up for Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period you can avoid a tax penalty by making your last HSA contribution the month before you turn 65. The reason is that you cannot contribute to an HSA once you have Medicare, and the handbook says to make your last contribution the month before your Part A coverage begins. Premium-free Part A goes back (retroactively) 6 months from when you sign up for Part A or apply for Social Security or RRB benefits, but no earlier than the first month you are eligible for Medicare, so that 6-month lookback is what moves the cut-off earlier in the chart's other rows, not in yours.

evidence.quote: You aren’t eligible to make contributions to an HSA after you have Medicare.
Consider making your last HSA contribution the month before your Part A coverage begins
You can avoid a tax penalty by making your last HSA contribution the month before you turn 65
Premium-free Part A coverage will go back (retroactively) 6 months from when you sign up for Part A or apply for benefits

question: Mom has Original Medicare and nothing else. Is there a cap on what she can be charged out of pocket in a year, and would a Medicare Advantage plan cap it?
expected_answer: Under Original Medicare there is no yearly limit on what she pays out of pocket unless she has supplemental coverage such as Medigap, Medicaid, or employer, retiree or union coverage. Medicare Advantage Plans do have a yearly limit on what you pay for covered Medicare services, which may include different limits for in-network and out-of-network services, and once she reached her plan's limit she would pay nothing for covered services for the rest of the year. The handbook gives no dollar amount for that limit.

evidence.quote: There’s no yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket, unless you have supplemental coverage—like Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap), Medicaid, employer, retiree, or union coverage.

question: My mother found a Medicare Advantage plan with a $0 monthly premium. Does that mean she would pay nothing each month for her Medicare?
expected_answer: No. A $0 plan premium does not remove the Part B premium: she still pays that every month, plus a Part A premium if she does not have premium-free Part A. If a plan does charge its own premium, she pays that on top of the Part B premium. Some Medicare Advantage Plans will help pay all or part of the Part B premium, sometimes called a "Medicare Part B premium reduction," so she should check whether that particular plan does.

evidence.quote: Some Medicare Advantage Plans have a $0 premium (but you still may pay the Part B premium).

You pay the monthly Part B premium and may also have to pay the plan’s premium. Some plans may have a $0 premium and may help pay all or part of your Part B premium.

question: My father takes several expensive prescriptions. Is there any cap on what he'll have to pay for his drugs in 2026?
expected_answer: Yes, if he has Medicare drug coverage (Part D). Yearly out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by his plan are capped at $2,100 in 2026. Once he reaches that cap, counting his own out-of-pocket spending plus certain payments other people or entities make, including Medicare's Extra Help program, he pays no copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year. The cap only covers drugs his plan covers.

evidence.quote: Your yearly out-of-pocket drug costs for drugs covered by your plan are capped at $2,100 in 2026.
you won’t have to pay a copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.

question: Does Medicare drug coverage pay for Eliquis? My mom wants to know before she picks a plan.
expected_answer: The handbook does not say. It states that information about a plan's list of covered drugs, called a formulary, is not included in the handbook because each plan has its own formulary, and that you should review a plan's formulary before joining. A correct answer says the handbook does not list covered drugs and points her to the plan itself or to Medicare.gov/plan-compare, and may add 1-800-MEDICARE or her State Health Insurance Assistance Program. It may also note that all plans must cover a wide range of drugs, including most drugs in certain protected classes.

evidence.quote: Information about a plan’s list of covered drugs (called a “formulary”) isn’t included in this handbook because each plan has its own formulary.

question: Dad is 68, has had Medicare since he was 65 and never joined a drug plan because he takes no medication. If he joins one now, will he be charged a penalty, and how is it worked out?
expected_answer: Yes, unless he had other creditable prescription drug coverage or gets Extra Help. The late enrollment penalty applies when you enroll after your Initial Enrollment Period is over and there was a period of 63 or more days in a row without Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage, and it is permanently added to the Part D premium for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage. The amount is 1% of the national base beneficiary premium ($38.99 in 2026) multiplied by the number of full, uncovered months, rounded to the nearest $0.10.

question: Dad is comparing Medigap Plan K and Plan L. What is the most each one would let him pay out of pocket in 2026, and how much of his costs do they cover?
expected_answer: In 2026 Plan K's yearly out-of-pocket limit is $8,000 and Plan L's is $4,000. After he meets that limit and the yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), the Medigap plan pays 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year. Until then, Plan K pays 50% and Plan L pays 75% of the Part B coinsurance or copayment, the blood benefit for the first 3 pints, the Part A hospice care coinsurance or copayment, skilled nursing facility care coinsurance, and the Part A deductible; both pay 100% of the Part A coinsurance and hospital costs, and neither covers the Part B deductible, Part B excess charges, or foreign travel emergency care.

question: When is the best time for my dad to buy a Medigap policy, and what happens if he waits?
expected_answer: The best time is his Medigap Open Enrollment Period, the 6-month period that begins the first month he has Medicare Part B and is 65 or older. After that period he may not be able to buy a Medigap policy at all, or it may cost more, although in certain situations he may have guaranteed issue rights outside it and some states have additional open enrollment periods. He must generally have both Part A and Part B before he can buy Medigap, and if he delays Part B because of group health coverage based on current employment, his Medigap Open Enrollment Period does not start until he gets Part B.

question: Dad signed up for Part B this past January. His doctor's office wants to book him for his annual wellness visit. Is he eligible for that yet, and what will it cost him?
expected_answer: Not yet. The yearly “Wellness” visit is only for people who have had Part B for longer than 12 months, and a first yearly “Wellness” visit can't take place within 12 months of Part B enrollment or of a “Welcome to Medicare” preventive visit. What he can get during the first 12 months he has Part B is the one-time “Welcome to Medicare” preventive visit, which is not a physical exam. He pays nothing for either visit if the doctor or other health care provider accepts assignment, but if the doctor does additional tests or services during the visit that Medicare doesn't cover under the preventive benefit (like a routine physical exam), he may owe coinsurance and the Part B deductible, or the full amount.

question: Mom's doctor wants to set up home health care after her hip surgery. What will Medicare charge her for it, and does she have to be bedridden to qualify?
expected_answer: She pays nothing for covered home health services; the only charge is for Medicare-covered durable medical equipment, where she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount and the Part B deductible applies. She does not have to be bedridden: “homebound” means she has trouble leaving home without help (a cane, wheelchair, walker, crutches, special transportation, or another person) because of an illness or injury, or leaving isn't recommended because of her condition, or leaving is normally a major effort. She also has to need part-time or intermittent skilled care — up to 8 hours a day combined, for a maximum of 28 hours each week (or up to 35 hours a week in some limited situations) — ordered by a doctor or other health care provider and given by a Medicare-certified home health agency.

evidence.quote: You pay nothing for covered home health services.

question: Mom's cancer is terminal and her doctor brought up hospice. Who has to sign off before Medicare will cover it, and what would she have to pay?
expected_answer: A hospice doctor and her own doctor (if she has one) must certify that she's terminally ill, meaning a life expectancy of 6 months or less, and she must sign a statement choosing hospice care instead of other Medicare-covered treatments for her terminal illness and related conditions. She pays nothing for hospice care, a copayment of up to $5 per prescription for outpatient drugs for pain and symptom management, and 5% of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite care, which she can get for up to 5 days at a time so her caregiver can rest. Medicare won't pay room and board in a facility unless the hospice medical team decides she needs short-term inpatient care to manage pain and other symptoms.

question: Dad needs a wheelchair to get around the house. Will Medicare buy him one, and what does he pay?
expected_answer: Medicare covers medically necessary durable medical equipment when a doctor or other health care provider orders it for use in the home, but he generally rents rather than buys: more expensive equipment like wheelchairs and hospital beds becomes his after 13 months of rental payments. He pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount and the Part B deductible applies. He should make sure the supplier accepts assignment of his claims for all rental months — if the claim isn't assigned he must pay the full cost of the equipment upfront and Medicare pays him back later for the amount it covers.

evidence.quote: Medicare covers medically necessary items like oxygen and oxygen equipment, walkers, and hospital beds when a doctor or other health care provider orders them for use in the home.

question: Mom has been badly depressed since Dad died and wants to see a therapist. Does Medicare cover that, and what will she pay?
expected_answer: Yes. Part B covers mental health care for conditions like depression and anxiety — counseling or psychotherapy, individually, in group or family settings, and in crisis situations — in outpatient settings including by telehealth, with a psychiatrist or other doctor, clinical psychologist, marriage and family therapist, mental health counselor, clinical nurse specialist, clinical social worker, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant. Generally she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount and the Part B deductible applies. She also pays coinsurance for each day of service she gets in a hospital outpatient setting or community mental health center.

question: My parents have Original Medicare. They're going to Portugal in June and to Puerto Rico in October. Would Medicare cover them if one of them ended up in the hospital on either trip?
expected_answer: Puerto Rico is covered; Portugal generally is not. Medicare generally doesn't cover health care while you're traveling outside the U.S., and for this rule “the U.S.” includes the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa — so Puerto Rico is not “outside the U.S.” There are some limited exceptions, and the handbook points to Medicare.gov/coverage/travel-outside-the-u.s. for them; the one it names is medically necessary ambulance transportation to a foreign hospital, covered only with admission for medically necessary covered inpatient hospital services, where they would pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount and the Part B deductible applies.

question: Mom spent three nights in the hospital but the billing office says she was under observation the whole time, never admitted. She needs a skilled nursing facility now. Will Part A pay for it?
expected_answer: No. Getting observation services without a formal inpatient admission makes her an outpatient even though she spent the nights in the hospital — she is an inpatient only when the hospital formally admits her with a doctor's order — and Part A skilled nursing facility care requires a 3-day minimum medically necessary inpatient hospital stay, not counting the day she leaves the hospital. Because she was under observation more than 24 hours, the hospital had to give her a “Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice” (also called “MOON”) explaining why she's an outpatient and how that affects what she pays in the hospital and for care after she leaves. Two exceptions could change the answer: the 3-day minimum may not apply if her doctor participates in an Accountable Care Organization approved for a Skilled Nursing Facility 3-Day Rule Waiver, and Medicare Advantage Plans may also waive it.

expected_answer: For days 61–90 he pays $434 each day. After day 150 he pays all costs.

question: My father moved to the U.S. at 58 and has only about 6 years of work here. Does he have to pay for Part A, how much in 2026, and what happens if he puts it off?
expected_answer: If he isn't eligible for premium-free Part A he may be able to buy it, and in 2026 he would pay a premium of either $311 or $565 each month, depending on how long he or his spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes. In most cases, if he buys Part A he must also have Part B and pay monthly premiums for both. If he doesn't buy Part A when he's first eligible, his monthly premium may go up 10%, and he'll have to pay the higher premium for twice the number of years he could have had Part A but didn't sign up — the handbook's example is 2 years without signing up meaning a 10% higher premium for 4 years.

question: Mom's only income is her Social Security check and she's struggling to pay her Medicare premiums. Is there a program that would help, and would it do anything for her drug costs?
expected_answer: She should apply for a Medicare Savings Program through her state; there are 4 kinds. Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB) covers Part A premiums (if she doesn't have premium-free Part A) and Part B premiums, and Medicare providers aren't allowed to bill her for covered services and items, including deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments; Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary (SLMB) covers the Part B premium only; Qualifying Individual (QI) covers the Part B premium only and is available only to people who don't qualify for any other Medicaid coverage or benefits; and Qualified Disabled and Working Individuals (QDWI) covers the Part A premium only. Income and resource limits vary by state, so she should contact her State Medical Assistance (Medicaid) office and apply even if she doesn't think she qualifies. If she qualifies for a QMB, SLMB, or QI program she qualifies automatically for Extra Help with her Medicare drug costs.

question: Dad is having a hernia repair next month in the hospital outpatient department. Exactly how many dollars will he owe for it?

question: Mom is in a Medicare Advantage plan and wants to move to a different one for next year. When can she make that change, and when would the new plan kick in?
expected_answer: During the Open Enrollment Period, October 15 to December 7 each year. In that window she can join, switch, or drop a Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage). Her coverage starts on January 1, as long as the plan gets her enrollment request by December 7.

question: Dad turned 65 three years ago and has Part A, but he never signed up for Part B and has no other coverage. He's signing up for Part B this February. Can he pick a Medicare Advantage plan at the same time?
expected_answer: Yes. If he has Part A coverage and gets Part B for the first time during the General Enrollment Period, January 1 to March 31, he can also join a Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage). He'll have 2 months after adding Part B to join a plan, and his coverage starts the first day of the month after he signs up. He must have both Part A and Part B to join a Medicare Advantage Plan.

question: Mom's house burned in a wildfire and in the chaos she missed her Medicare sign-up window. Is there any way for her to enroll now, and how soon after that could she get a drug plan?
expected_answer: She may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period for an exceptional situation: the handbook says you may be eligible if you miss an enrollment period because of circumstances like being impacted by a natural disaster or an emergency, incarceration, employer or health plan error, losing Medicaid coverage, or other circumstances outside your control that Medicare determines are exceptional. If she signs up for Part A or Part B during a Special Enrollment Period because of an exceptional circumstance, she then has 2 months to join a Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage) or a Medicare drug plan. That coverage starts the first day of the month after the plan gets her request to join. The handbook tells her to visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE for more information.

question: Mom joined a Medicare Advantage plan in January and already regrets it. It's now February. Can she move to a different plan, and how many times can she change?
expected_answer: Yes. The Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period runs January 1 to March 31, and during it someone already in a Medicare Advantage Plan can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage), or drop the plan and return to Original Medicare and also join a separate Medicare drug plan. She can only make one change during this period. She can't use this period to switch from Original Medicare to a Medicare Advantage Plan, to join a separate drug plan if she has Original Medicare, or to switch from one Medicare drug plan to another if she has Original Medicare.

evidence.quote: Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period January 1 to March 31 Note: You can only switch plans once during this period.

Switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage). • Drop your Medicare Advantage Plan and return to Original Medicare. You’ll also be able to join a separate Medicare drug plan.
During this period, you can’t: • Switch from Original Medicare to a Medicare Advantage Plan. • Join a separate Medicare drug plan if you have Original Medicare.

question: Mom sees a cardiologist regularly and has a stress test every year. If she moves from Original Medicare to a Medicare Advantage plan, will she suddenly need referrals and pre-approvals she doesn't need now?
expected_answer: Probably, on both counts. Under Original Medicare, in most cases she doesn't need a referral to use a specialist, and in most cases she doesn't need approval (prior authorization) for Original Medicare to cover her services or supplies. Under a Medicare Advantage Plan, she may need to get a referral to use a specialist and may need to get approval (prior authorization) from the plan before it covers certain services or supplies. She may also need to use doctors and other providers in the plan's network and service area for non-emergency care, with out-of-network coverage, where a plan offers it, typically costing more.

evidence.quote: In most cases, you don’t need a referral to use a specialist. You may need to get a referral to use a specialist.

In most cases, you don't need approval (prior authorization) for Original Medicare to cover your services or supplies.

question: Mom is down to two Medicare Advantage plans, an HMO and a PPO. Would she have to pick a primary care doctor or get referrals, and what happens if she sees a doctor outside the network?
expected_answer: With the HMO she generally must get her care from doctors, other health care providers, or hospitals in the plan's network (except emergency care, out-of-area urgent care, or temporary out-of-area dialysis); in most cases she must choose a primary care doctor and in most cases needs a referral to see a specialist, though certain services like yearly mammogram screenings don't require one. If she gets non-emergency care outside the HMO's network without authorization she may have to pay the full cost, unless it is an HMO Point-of-Service (HMOPOS) plan, which may let her get some out-of-network services for a higher copayment or coinsurance. With the PPO she can use out-of-network providers for covered services, usually for a higher cost, if the provider agrees to treat her and hasn't opted out of Medicare; she does not need to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases she does not need a referral, although using in-network specialists usually costs less.

evidence.quote: You generally must get your care and services from doctors, other health care providers, or hospitals in the plan’s network

question: How much is the monthly premium for the Medicare Advantage HMO plan my mother wants to join in Cook County, Illinois?
expected_answer: The handbook does not list premiums for individual plans. It explains only how Medicare Advantage costs work — some plans have a $0 premium, you still pay the Part B premium, and any plan premium is paid in addition to it — and it says to contact the plan or visit Medicare.gov/plan-compare to learn your costs in a specific Medicare Advantage Plan and to get specific plan costs. A correct answer says the figure isn't in the handbook and names Medicare.gov/plan-compare or the plan itself (1-800-MEDICARE or a State Health Insurance Assistance Program are also acceptable).

evidence.quote: To learn more about your costs in a specific Medicare Advantage Plan, contact the plan or visit Medicare.gov/plan-compare.
Visit Medicare.gov/plan-compare to get specific Medicare drug plan and Medicare Advantage Plan costs, and call the plans you’re interested in to get more details.

question: Mom has a high income and gets her drug coverage through a Medicare Advantage plan. Does she still owe the Part D extra charge, and does she pay it to the plan?
expected_answer: Yes, she still owes it, and no, she does not pay it to the plan. If her income is above the limit (in 2026, $109,000 filing individually or $218,000 married filing jointly) she pays an extra amount on top of her plan premium, sometimes called “Part D IRMAA,” and she has to pay it even though she's in a Medicare Advantage Plan that includes drug coverage. Usually Medicare or the Railroad Retirement Board deducts it from her Social Security or RRB payment; if she's billed for it instead, she must pay Medicare or the RRB, not her plan, and she pays it separately even if an employer or another third party pays her plan premium. If she doesn't pay it she could lose her Part D coverage, may not be able to join another plan right away, and may have to pay a late enrollment penalty.

question: Mom takes insulin every day. Is there a limit on what her Medicare drug plan can charge her for it, and does she have to meet her deductible first?
expected_answer: Yes to the limit and no to the deductible: plans can't charge her more than $35 for a one-month supply of each Part D-covered insulin she takes, and she doesn't have to pay a deductible for insulin. Part D covers insulin, including insulin used with either a disposable or non-traditional insulin pump, and certain medical supplies used to inject it, like syringes, gauze, and alcohol swabs; covered insulin products are included on her plan's formulary. Similar caps on costs apply for traditional insulin used in Part B-covered insulin pumps.

evidence.quote: Plans can’t charge you more than $35 for a one-month supply of each Part D-covered insulin you take, and you don’t have to pay a deductible for insulin.

question: Dad's drug plan puts his medicine on an expensive tier and his doctor says the cheaper ones won't work for him. Can he ask the plan to charge him less, and how does that work?
expected_answer: Yes. If his drug is in a higher tier and his prescriber thinks he needs it instead of a similar drug in a lower tier, he or his prescriber can ask the plan for an exception to get a lower coinsurance or copayment for the higher-tier drug. He or his prescriber must contact the plan to ask for a coverage determination or an exception; for a prescription he hasn't gotten yet, either of them can make a standard request or an expedited (fast) request by phone or in writing, and the request will be expedited if the plan determines, or his prescriber tells the plan, that his life or health may be at risk by waiting. When he requests an exception, his prescriber must provide a statement explaining the medical reason why the plan should approve it.

question: What's the most a Medicare drug plan is allowed to charge for its yearly deductible in 2026?
expected_answer: The handbook does not give that limit. All it says about the yearly deductible is what it is — the amount you must pay before your plan begins to pay its share of your covered drugs — plus that some plans don't have one and that in some plans that do, drugs on some tiers are covered before the deductible; it prints no maximum anywhere. It says drug costs vary based on the plan you choose and sends you to Medicare.gov/plan-compare for specific Medicare drug plan costs. A correct answer says the maximum isn't in the handbook and points to Medicare.gov/plan-compare, the plan itself, or 1-800-MEDICARE.

question: Dad is choosing between Medigap Plan N and a high-deductible Plan G. What extra out-of-pocket costs does each of those carry in 2026?
expected_answer: Plan N pays 100% of the Part B coinsurance, but he must pay a copayment of up to $20 for some office visits and up to a $50 copayment for emergency room visits that don't result in an inpatient admission. Plans F and G also offer a high-deductible version in some states: with it, he must pay Medicare-covered costs (coinsurance, copayments, and deductibles) up to the deductible amount of $2,950 in 2026 before the policy pays anything. He should also know he can't buy Plan C or Plan F at all if he was new to Medicare on or after January 1, 2020.

question: Dad has had a Medigap policy for years but wants to try a Medicare Advantage plan. If he hates it, can he get his Medigap policy back?
expected_answer: If he drops a Medigap policy to join a Medicare Advantage Plan for the first time, he gets a single 12-month period — his trial right period — to get that Medigap policy back if the same insurance company still sells it once he returns to Original Medicare. If it isn't available, he can buy certain Medigap policies, depending on state law and whether he was new to Medicare on or after January 1, 2020, and he may also have an opportunity to join a Medicare drug plan at that time. Two practical points: most Medigap policies don't automatically cancel when he joins a Medicare Advantage Plan, so he has to contact his insurance company, and he can't use Medigap to pay his Medicare Advantage Plan's copayments, deductibles, and premiums.

question: How much would a Medigap Plan G policy cost my dad per month?
expected_answer: The handbook does not print Medigap premiums. It says the costs can vary between plans offered by different companies for exactly the same coverage and may go up as you get older, that some states limit Medigap premium costs, and that a Medigap policy only covers one person so spouses must buy separate coverage. For an actual price it sends you to Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans to find policies and pricing in your area. A correct answer says the figure isn't in the handbook and names that page, his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP), his State Insurance Department, or a trusted agent or broker.
